lesson.title: One Collision, One Step: Elementary Steps
lesson.summary: An elementary step is a single molecular-level event, one collision or one decomposition, and it is the one situation where you can write a rate law directly from the balanced equation instead of measuring it.
lesson.body:
Everything you have learned about reaction rate and rate laws up to this point comes with an important warning: for an overall balanced chemical equation, you cannot assume the exponents in the rate law match the equation's stoichiometric coefficients. If a reaction is written as 2A + B, you cannot assume the rate law is k[A]^2[B] just because those are the coefficients; the true rate law has to be measured experimentally. That warning exists because most balanced equations describe the net result of several distinct molecular events happening in sequence, not one single event.

An elementary step is different: it describes one specific molecular-level event, either a single molecule breaking apart or rearranging, or a specific set of particles colliding and reacting directly, with nothing hidden and no intermediate stages folded in. Because an elementary step describes exactly what physically collides, you genuinely can write its rate law straight from its own coefficients, since those coefficients tell you exactly how many of each particle need to come together for that particular event to occur. This is the one exception to the "always measure it" rule, and it is an exception precisely because an elementary step is not a summary of several events, it is one event.

For example, consider the elementary step:

2 NO(g) + O2(g) -> 2 NO2(g)

If this really is a single elementary step, meaning two NO molecules and one O2 molecule all come together in one collision event, then its rate law follows directly from its coefficients:

rate = k[NO]^2[O2]

The exponent 2 on [NO] reflects the fact that two NO molecules have to be present and colliding for this specific step to happen, and the exponent 1 on [O2] reflects the one O2 molecule involved. This is a genuinely different logical move than the method of initial rates you use for overall reactions: here, the exponents come from counting particles in a proposed molecular event, not from running experiments and comparing rates.

This distinction sets up the next several chapters. A full reaction mechanism is a proposed sequence of elementary steps, written one after another, that together add up to the overall balanced equation; you will see exactly how that summation works, and how it explains an overall reaction's true rate law, in the Reaction Mechanisms chapter. The number of particles that come together in one elementary step, whether it is one, two, or (rarely) three, has its own name: molecularity, which gets its own dedicated treatment shortly. Keep both of these ideas in mind together: an elementary step is a real, physically meaningful molecular event, and its rate law is one of the few places in kinetics where you are allowed to read exponents straight off a chemical equation.
